planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall into lean, dry, sandy to rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; the thick taproot makes transplanting unreliable after the first year, so choose a permanent spot.

directions: Pale four o'clock is a clump-forming perennial of dry, rocky, and sandy prairies across the central Great Plains, including the limestone-derived soils of the Flint Hills, where it persists on roadsides and grazed pastures that would defeat less drought-hardy forbs. Branching stems carry pairs of gray-green, finely hairy leaves and clusters of small, pale pink to white, trumpet-shaped flowers that open in late afternoon and through the evening, attracting hawkmoths and other night-flying pollinators before closing again the next morning. A thick, woody taproot stores water and carbohydrates, giving the plant exceptional heat and drought tolerance once established but making container culture or transplanting difficult. Use it in a dry, sunny prairie border or gravel garden where its understated summer-long bloom and low maintenance needs are an asset rather than planting it where a showier, more compact habit is required.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, very well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; this low taprooted species establishes best from seed sown in place rather than from transplants.

directions: Shaggy dwarf morning glory forms a dense, silvery mat of small, hairy, gray-green leaves hugging the ground on dry, rocky prairie hillsides and limestone outcrops across the Great Plains, including the Flint Hills. From late spring through summer it produces a steady succession of small, sky-blue, funnel-shaped flowers that open in the morning and close by early afternoon, giving a long season of color despite each individual bloom being short-lived. Its deep, slender taproot allows it to shrug off drought and heat that would stress most low groundcovers, and it rarely needs supplemental water once settled in. Use it between flagstones, along the edge of a gravel path, or in a rock garden where its tight, low habit and repeat-blooming blue flowers can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Scatter seed in fall directly among established native bunchgrasses such as little bluestem or sideoats grama; Castilleja is hemiparasitic on grass roots and fails to thrive without a living host nearby.

directions: Downy paintbrush is a hemiparasitic perennial of dry mixed-grass and tallgrass prairie from the Canadian plains south through the Flint Hills region to Texas and New Mexico, tapping into the roots of neighboring prairie grasses for part of its water and nutrients rather than growing as a fully self-sufficient plant. Unlike the familiar scarlet-bracted eastern paintbrushes, its elongated bracts and tubular flowers are pale cream, greenish-yellow, or lavender-tinged, a coloring thought to be adapted to hawkmoth pollinators rather than the hummingbirds that favor redder paintbrush species. Blooming in mid-spring, its soft gray-green, finely divided foliage and pastel flower spikes are easy to overlook until established, but a well-sited planting rewards patience with a long-lived, low-maintenance addition to a native grass meadow. Establish only by interseeding with a compatible host grass, never alone in bare or tilled soil, and avoid fertile or heavily amended soil that discourages the hemiparasitic relationship.

planting.note: Sow seed on the soil surface in fall and allow natural winter cold-moist stratification; early buttercup is slow to establish from seed but persists for years once a clump is settled in open prairie or light-shaded turf.

directions: Early buttercup is one of the first wildflowers to bloom on Flint Hills prairie hillsides and dry open woodland edges, sending up tufted rosettes of deeply lobed, hairy leaves and glossy, varnish-bright yellow five-petaled flowers as early as March. Its thickened, fascicled roots (giving the species its name) store enough reserve for the plant to flower and set seed quickly before summer heat and competition from taller prairie grasses arrive, after which the foliage yellows and the plant goes dormant until the following spring. This short, predictable above-ground season makes it a good companion for interplanting at the sunny edge of a prairie planting or beneath deciduous shrubs, where it fills an early-spring gap without competing with summer bloomers later in the year. It spreads modestly by seed and offsets but is not aggressive, making it suitable for naturalizing in a native lawn alternative or meadow matrix.
